new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata: 'A Grammar of Akajeru', Zamponi & Comrie, 186 pp.). Fresh extracted text of PDF page 35 (printed p. 22, running foot '22 A GRAMMAR OF AKAJERU') gives sec. '2.2 Stress' exactly as quoted: 'Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemi-cally relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily.' Only difference is the line-break hyphen in 'phonemi-cally'. line 1318-1323 agrees; the index (line 7872) lists 'stress 22' as the only stress entry; the sole other hit is ch. 4 endnote 7 ( line 2583, printed p. 50): PGA orsub…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive in any Great Andamanese language; predictable, non-phonemic prominence falls on the first syllable of the root (after any prefixes), normally.
new_statements.exceptions: None specific; hedged with 'at least ordinarily'. (For PGA, the sibling-held Yadav 1985: 196 reports strong final accent on vocatives and exclamations; not stated for Bo.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, non-phonemic; stated for the root (Great Andamanese words carry somatic/class prefixes, so root-initial is not necessarily word-initial). The statement is a family-wide generalization by the authors; Akabo itself is attested only by 18 words and a few names in Radcliffe-Brown 1933, which do not mark stress, so no Akabo-specific stress data exist.
new_statements.identity_note: Akabo (Aka-Bo, Temple's 'Tabo') is attested only by 18 words and a few names in Radcliffe-Brown 1933; Zamponi & Comrie 2021: 13 conclude Akabo and Akajeru (akaj1239) 'were undoubtedly mutually intelligible dialects of the same language'. The quoted stress statement is the authors' family-wide generalization (all Great Andamanese languages incl. Present Great Andamanese), made in the Akajeru grammar, not a description of Akabo data. Temple 1903: 115 ('on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem') is an Aka-Bea-based rule that explicitly excludes the then-unstudied Bo.

Sec. 1.3.2 (pp. 12-13): Akabo survives only as 18 words + a few names in Radcliffe-Brown 1933; Akabo and Akajeru 'were undoubtedly mutually intelligible dialects of the same language'. Ch. 4 endnote 7 (p. 50): PGA orshubi heard 'as a single word with initial stress'.

sources.note: p. 115 (the scanned text): 'Peculiarities of Speech. -- Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem.' But p. 116 sec. V: 'Of the Five Languages of the Northern (Yerewa) Group, two, Kora and Tabo, are still quite unstudied' -- Temple's 'Tabo' is Aka-Bo, so his rule rests on South Andamanese (Aka-Bea) data and explicitly excludes Bo.
